starting_points: Test level, register/voicing, timing, note length, and arrangement role before carving permanent spectral holes.
When EQ is justified, begin broad and modest—often about 1–2 dB as a diagnostic move—then level-match and adjust by ear.
Use dynamic processing only when the collision is demonstrably intermittent and preserve tone between events.
stop_rule: Stop or back off when the target cue becomes clear but the supporting source loses useful body, character, blend, or mono stability.
teaching_principle: Frequency allocation is role, register, timing, envelope, level, and spectrum working together; EQ is only one possible last-mile tool.
title: When should I rewrite or revoice a part instead of EQing it
tradeoffs_and_risks: Creating spectral space can remove useful body, blend, realism, or source identity.
Dynamic or multiband methods add timing, crossover, and detector complexity.
Stereo separation may collapse in mono and does not solve center masking reliably.
undo_or_reset: Restore the preserved regions, mutes, levels, voicings, automation, or project alternative and replay the same section.

what_to_listen_for: The obscured cue—pitch, lyric, attack, body, rhythm, or texture—should become clearer in the full mix.
The supporting source should retain enough body, character, and role rather than sounding hollow or disconnected.
The improvement should survive matched loudness and, where relevant, mono or small-speaker checks.
